speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAYS' LINE TO YUKON-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity and ask for unanimous consent of the House to a motion which seeks to end the uncertainty and the concern of all residents of northeastern British Columbia over the fact that a vital section of the British Columbia Railway may be abandoned.
Having regard to the fact that the entire industrial base supporting the town of Fort Nelson as well as the general area of northern British Columbia relies almost exclusively on the railway for its survival, and considering that the abandonment of this railway from Fort St. John to Fort Nelson would place in jeopardy several hundreds of jobs, and further considering the importance of that section of the BCR in the context of the northwestern rail authority as recommended by Mr. Justice Hall, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke):
That the government enter into discussions with the province of British Columbia immediately with the view of applying the resources and jurisdiction of the federal government not only to prevent the abandonment of the British Columbia Railways' northern line but to plan, jointly with the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, the extension of this rail line to the Yukon and the establishment of certain interchange connections with other northwestern railways, in order to accommodate such industrial development schemes as the Alaska Highway pipeline which are already committed for the area.

subsubtopic: FAMILY IN U.S.S.R. PREVENTED FROM EMIGRATING TO ISRAEL- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion concerns the detention of a family in the Soviet Union. In 1970, Vladimir Slepak applied to Soviet authorities to emigrate to Israel. He was refused permission on the grounds that he had been involved in secret work. Since then, Mr. Slepak has been harassed, refused employment and imprisoned. His wife, who is a qualified radiologist, also has been refused employment. One of their sons has gone into hiding in order to avoid being drafted into the army; another son has fled the country altogether. In view of this totally inhumane treatment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That this House direct the Secretary of State for External Affairs to discuss with Soviet authorities the possibility of the Slepak family being allowed to leave the Soviet Union and take up residence in Israel.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF SALES TAX PROPOSALS ON QUEBEC INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. As a result of the first ministers' conference in February it was decided to set up some 22 consultative task forces on Canadian manufacturing with representation from the provinces, business and the federal government. The government prepared a document for them setting out their policies, objectives and comments on the manufacturing sector. I refer to page 11 of that document, which reads as follows:
In the Quebec manufacturing sector the overriding issue is one of adjustment to competitive pressures on the traditional sectors-textiles, clothing, footwear and furniture.
Also, it states that average manufacturing employment in Canada dropped by 34,000 last year, with 30,000 of those a net loss in Quebec in those sectors. My question to the Prime Minister is: In view of these findings by the government as expressed in the government's own official documents, why is the government opposing the suggestion of the province of Quebec that the sales tax be eliminated in the areas of textiles, clothing, footwear and furniture, which would therefore help Quebec consumers in those areas to spend more and encourage those manufacturing sectors and manufacturing employment in Quebec? Why does the government continue to oppose this?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF SALES TAX PROPOSALS ON QUEBEC INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has misunderstood the government's position. We have not opposed this; on the contrary, I have said repeatedly that we understood the Quebec government taking these steps to bolster its own particular industry. Therefore, we are not opposing it. Obviously, this is a tax within provincial jurisdiction. They are free to cut those taxes, as indeed other provinces have increased and cut taxes in other areas. We know of one province which has no sales tax at all. This is entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Not only do we not oppose it, but we supported it in other ways: we have brought in quotas; there are tariffs which exist; there are many measures of direct support from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which have been made to these sectors so that jobs could be created and retained in that area. It is a misunderstanding to say we are opposed to it. What we do say is that if the province wants to do that by its own budget, with its own tax resources, we applaud it. If it wants to co-operate with the federal government in a series of tax measures that will help the whole

country and not only industries in one province, then this is what we proposed on budget night.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I reply briefly to the hon. member's remarks in moving concurrence of this report. Without in any way getting into a contretemps, may I say that I had hoped I might have more notice that this report would be called at three o'clock today. However, I want to second the hon. member's remarks regarding the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), the chairman of the committee, and I want to compliment both that hon. member and all members of the committee on the work that they did in committee on the subject of pornography, which has concerned all members of the House and which certainly has been of great concern to myself and to my officials as well as to officials of the Department of National Revenue who are responsible for policing of the Customs Act. Also, it has been of great concern

April 19, 1978
Justice and Legal Affairs
to provincial attorneys general with whom I have discussed this subject on a number of occasions, and to local police forces who are responsible for the enforcement of laws at the local level.
The committee has done a great deal of work and its report is a valuable document. Therefore, we on this side will be supporting the hon. member's motion. However, in doing so I want to place several caveats on the record. As the committee has been advised, and as I have been advised by a formal communication from the provincial attorneys general, they would not like to see this subject legislated without having the opportunity to make further representations. We discussed this matter at the federal-provincial meeting of attorneys general last fall. The provincial attorneys general had a further discussion on the subject and they indicated to me that they wanted some changes made but that they would forward to me their concrete proposals.
During the course of the committee's hearings and proceedings I received a communication from the provincial attorneys general to the effect that they wanted to discuss changes in the law relating to pornography, first, at the federal-provincial conference of attorneys general to be held in July and, second, at the meeting of the commissioners of uniformity which will be held in August. Ever since I have been Minister of Justice I have introduced amendments to the Criminal Code only after consultation with provincial attorneys general who, after all, are responsible for the enforcement of the laws that we write here.
There are two recommendations of the committee that give me some concern. I do not have the committee's report in front of me, but one recommendation relates to the fact that the provincial attorneys general may be empowered under the Criminal Code to order that a person accused of producing, manufacturing or distributing pornography be subject to trial by judge and jury only. That is to say, a provincial attorney general, in spite of the election of the accused to be tried by a judge, may order that he be tried by judge and jury.
The second area deals with the calling of expert witnesses in a pornography trial. In such a trial, expert witnesses as to what community standards are will not be allowed to testify. I have some real grave reservations about that. It is one matter which I am considering and thinking about a great deal. It is a matter on which I want to consult the provincial attorneys general. There is a question as to whether that recommendation, if enacted in the Criminal Code, would not be contrary to the Bill of Rights, which provides that people are entitled to due process and a full and fair defence. I know this matter troubled the committee a great deal, and I know its recommendations have been made in very good conscience. On both sides of that committee, very good lawyers are represented.
What has been fundamental to our system of law is that an accused person is entitled to put to the court, or to the court and the jury, the fullest possible defence. It is up to a jury to weigh whether that defence is any good or not, and then make

its judgment. At this point, without further consideration and study I am very hesitant about adopting the proposal that the accused is not entitled to call experts. I have some concern and fear that in fact it is contrary to the Bill of Rights.
I agree with the concern expressed by the committee in the substance of the report. In a statement to the committee, I indicated my concern about the issue. I hope to be able to introduce amendments to the Criminal Code very shortly, as I indicated to the committee. These amendments would deal with the recommendations of the committee's report, deal with the question of the definition of pornography, deal with the question of the use of children in the manufacturing and portrayal of pornography, and the banning of certain explicit acts by children in the production of pornography. I hope to introduce amendments which would increase the penalties applicable to both the manufacturing and distribution of pornography. In fact, I hope to introduce those amendments very shortly. In reacting to my concern about the issue of pornography, the concern of provincial attorneys general, and the concern expressed in the committee's unanimous report, I hope to introduce those amendments shortly.
Generally we on this side of the house would support the hon. member's motion, but I wanted to make those two caveats. I am not privy as to how long this parliament will be sitting, but I hope to have an opportunity to introduce the amendments of which I speak. I look forward to hearing the reactions of provincial attorneys general to the specific amendments I am proposing, which would result in the Criminal Code being amended to deal more effectively with the question of pornography. I indicated that in my statement before the committee, and it was indicated in the report of the committee.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very happy to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) indicate that he would second the motion of concurrence in this report, which was the unanimous report of all parties. As has been stated by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), we have attended many meetings and we have heard many witnesses.
It was refreshing to see the Minister of Justice displaying this afternoon that flexibility he can exercise on many occasions. When he came before us and gave his first statement, he was of the opinion that the definition of pornography under the Criminal Code was adequate. If we check the precedents in reference to that definition, we will find that was the greatest part of the inadequacy in reference to our study of this report. When one is dealing with community standards, one must remember that community standards differ from one place to another. I was most happy to see that now we have a Minister of Justice, even if he is leaving us, who is flexible enough during the short period of time between now and the election. He has changed his mind and now believes the report is correct, that we require a new definition of pornography.
In reference to the two reservations which were mentioned under the caveat he was filing, I emphasize the report recommended that only expert witnesses would not be able to testify in reference to community standards. We in this party believe
April 19, 1978

the jury system is fundamental to the freedom and liberty of the subject. If we are to use the words "community standards" in any definition, then it should be a decision made by juries without confusion from various experts. On the other hand, the report was most silent in reference to calling expert witnesses regarding other definitions or matters referring to pornography.
In reference to the question of trial by judge and jury, I am sure the Minister of Justice, with his wisdom, knowledge and expertise, as well as that of people within his department, is well aware that an indictable offence of this nature falling under the proper part of the Criminal Code, after some teeth have been put into the act, would mean that anyone could be tried by judge and jury throughout the country. Election by judge alone would not be legal under the Criminal Code as it stands now. Thus, there would be no real fundamental change.
The only province which would experience a change is the province of Alberta, from whence I come. That is the only province in Canada that can eliminate the jury, even on a serious murder trial. The reason for that is no one has ever amended the Northwest Territories Act which is incorporated in the Criminal Code. It was incorporated there because at the time the Northwest Territories Act was drafted there were not enough people in Alberta to gather together 12 good men and women to form a jury. The population of Calgary now is growing at the rate of 3,000 per month, so it is obvious that problem has been overcome.
I am happy to see the Minister of Justice has endorsed the report, has changed his opinion, has been very flexible, and is ready now, as he has done, to second this report, which was a unanimous study by all members of the House. I believe this report will be accepted across the land as a step in the right direction to stop the filth factory of material which is being imported from the United States into Canada.
It was shown in committee that $20 million was made in the maritimes alone from the sale of periodicals, magazines and other types of equipment which were studied by members of the committee. Perhaps the minister is straddling the line when he agrees and votes for the report, and files these caveats. I hope he does not straddle it too far, but stays with the unanimous recommendations of the report. We do not want half a piece of pie; the committee recommended that we get the whole pie and eat it.

Mr. Speaker, I was a member of this particular committee and I have no hesitation in supporting the bald recommendations on changes to the Criminal Code. However, I have severe hesitation in accepting some of the rhetoric which went into the report and which is not relevant to the actual changes recommended by the committee.
I should like to review the specific changes recommended by the committee so that we do not mislead the press; the press is easily confused on this particular subject. The specific changes in the report dealt with the creation of a new section on child pornography. My party supports that change. It did not ban
Justice and Legal Affairs
the testimony of expert witnesses entirely, but that testimony was banned in a limited sense. It dealt with the evidence that could be put forward to a jury regarding current community standards, which continue to be the criteria for cases of this nature. There is no ban in this report, as the press unfortunately has reported frequently, on the calling of any expert witnesses on the subject. What the committee decided was that to determine community standards a jury is a better forum than to allow someone from a university, who may not be as familiar with those community standards, to make a report with regard to them.
The private members' bills that were submitted to this committee represented a great case of overkill. In fact, if those private members' bills had been allowed to pass we probably would have wound up banning the bible since it specifically describes acts which would clearly have come within the changes that were contemplated by several members of this House in terms of the Criminal Code.
To show how dangerous this particular subject can be, when we look at the question of what we can control and what we cannot control, the decision of the Ontario censorship board in which it banned a movie called "Pretty Baby" is a classic case-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: And rightly so.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is a movie that has tremendous literary merit, a movie that the people of Ontario will no doubt see by simply crossing the river to Hull, making a lot of money for some people in Quebec. I am not against that, but that same censorship board approved a movie called "Taxi Driver" and that movie dealt almost exclusively with violence, sex and teenage prostitution. The movie the board banned dealt with the subject of a child who in her early years matured in a house of prostitution but was able somehow to come out of that grime and have a successful life. There is an interesting story in the Louis Malle movie.
This is the difficulty when members of parliament start sitting in judgment on matters that have great artistic merit. There is always an agony in this business in determining whether there really is sexual exploitation, or whether there is literary merit in what happens.
Therefore, I support the bald recommendations of the committee, but I stand here warning the committee and the minister that when it comes to changes in the Criminal Code which deal with censorship we should not ban those things which have classic literary merit, and that judgment is always going to be a discretionary judgment. It is not going to work if you apply the standards of some small community to the whole province in respect of what the people can or cannot see.
We are not opposed, of course, to increasing the penalties that are involved, but we are opposed to a present law, the Customs Act, that allows a customs officer, with no experience whatsoever as to what has literary merit, to decide on his own that a certain publication is unworthy for the eyes of Canadi-

Eldon wants to know which side I am on. He is always confused in this place. When you make this kind of decision the matter should not be considered in the simplistic way in which private members have advanced, that somehow all you have to do is ban the description of the sexual act and that will solve all our problems in respect of pornography. That will not happen. There has to be a judgment decision. Otherwise works of literary merit in this country and in our heritage would all be banned, and the great art of history would be banned. That is what will happen if you paint this subject with a broad brush.
If I can go back to the narrow question of the specific recommendations that were made by the committee, they are largely supportive of the position taken by the province of British Columbia which left the question of undue exploitation to the decision of a judge and jury. In this case it would now be left to the jury. I agree with that recommendation. There must be some kind of subjective decision in respect of what is or is not pornography.
It is pointed out that child pornography is a very special matter, and that the abuse of children is something that should be placed under control. We support that recommendation. We support the recommendations about increasing the penalty. However, there is a good deal of rhetoric, and if this were taken to its logical conclusion-and I am not talking about changes to the Criminal Code which the committee recommended and which are sound and wise-we would be banning anything that offends someone. As a result we would find that the cultural heritage of this country would become a pretty thin thing indeed. That will happen if we overreact on this subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the giving of concurrence in this motion, and I sense that, following the lead of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the House will shortly be ready to do that. However, I do think it appropriate that I make a few comments.
I begin by thanking those hon. members who have made comments of personal commendation. Personally, I feel that the lion's share of credit should go to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and those other members on all sides of the House who put forward the bills which enabled the committee to deal with the problem that is the subject matter of this report.
I want to say a few words because this is a subject in respect of which rhetoric is of some importance. I agree with the comment of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) that one must not confuse the recommendations and the rhetoric either of the report or of any other speaker in this
[Mr. Leggatt.)
House. Nevertheless, I think it is very important to observe that the committee, in making its recommendations, on the one hand is not greatly extending the law that exists in radically new directions, but on the other hand is considerably deepening the law, if I may put it that way, in respect of the rights of two target groups who have not always been considered in our legislation. Those two groups are women and children.
Having regard to children, the recommendations of the committee are obviously there for all to see; they are to protect children from exposure to the material and also to protect them from being exploited by being involved in its production.
Having regard to women, I think the point has been missed by some of those in the media who have criticised our report. It is important to realize that the changes in the law and in the definition of the law which we have suggested, other than those aimed at protecting children, are particularly aimed at bringing the woman's point of view into our law in this area for the first time.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That was our purpose in introducing the concept of the degradation of the human person, which expressed the views of women witnesses who appeared before us and who wrote us from across the country.
It was also the purpose behind broadening the definition through severing the link which previously had to be found between violence and sex, and the other categories and sex, and to say that even if sex were not involved, these other categories of crime and horror and violence could in themselves be considered to be obscenity when there is undue exploitation. The purpose the committee had in mind was to give protection in this branch of the law, for the first time, to the sensibilities of women, as the principal target group of most pornography.
If I may say so, I believe the people of Canada have a much more basic understanding of this issue than those who have written, accusing us of all kinds of intellectual and moral sins, comparing us to Cromwell, Mao Tse-Tung and others in history who perhaps are often thought of as having less savoury reputations. The people, as my own constituents have manifested, support such legislation very strongly, and I am sure that the members of this House who were involved in this study have received a great deal of support for the recommendations which we have made.
It is with a sense of pride that all of us who were involved with this subject can stand before the House and present this report and vote its concurrence.

subsubtopic: HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS ACT
speechtext: Since January 1, 1977, has the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs banned or recommended against the use of (a) clothing because of its flammability (b) medicine containers because of danger to small children?

speakeroldname: Mr. Alan G. Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS ACT
speechtext: (a) November 2, 1971, all textile fibre products for consumer use that are hazardously flammable were banned from advertisement, sale or importation into Canada under the Hazardous Products Act. At the same time, a separate more stringent minimum flammability level was established for children's sleepwear and on April 1, 1972, articles of bedding (blankets, sheets, bedspreads, etc.) were similarly regulated at the more stringent level. Approximately five clothing products were seized in 1977. (b) As medicines come within the purview of the Food and Drugs Act, the packaging of such products falls within the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare Canada. CCA did, however, amend the Hazardous Products (Hazardous Substances) Regs, on July 21, 1977 so that household products containing toxic amounts of petroleum distillates, turpentine, methyl alcohol and pine oil be packaged in child-resistant containers. The amendment specifies that as of October 1, 1978, affected products packaged on or after July 15, 1977 must be packaged in child-resistant containers. Prior to the above amendment, the Hazardous Products (Hazardous Substances) Regulations required child-resistant containers on certain corrosive drain cleaners, cyanoacrylate adhesives and certain liquid wood furniture polishes.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, April 18, consideration of the motion by Mr. Chretien that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now back to the main budget motion. What I
April 19, 1978

am going to do today is put forward what I think are the good features of the budget and some of the features which are not so good.
First, the good news. I want to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for putting into the budget amendments to the registered retirement savings plan provisions to make them more flexible and thereby attract more savings. When I spoke on this matter two years ago and made the proposal to the then minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Macdonald, he said he would put the matter before the committee that served him in the Department of Finance and get their judgment on it. I was very pleased to see it in the budget two years later.
To give an idea of the importance of this matter, it should be remembered that just seven years ago about 360,000 Canadians invested in registered retirement savings plans. In his budget address the minister said there are now nearly two million, a six-fold increase in seven years. With these amendments I think that over the next five or ten years we can look forward not only to a 20 per cent increase but to as high as 40 or 50 per cent. This not only helps the individual to save for his later years in addition to the universal programs that are in place, but it provides the nation with more capital with which to finance the heavy capital intensive programs we face in the next two or three decades.
The other advantage is that the more people who put money into this type of program, the greater the stabilizing effect on the economy. I think it is clear that the advantage finally rests with the person who puts money into this type of savings.
In particular, I should like to commend the minister on the addition not only of the set number of years mentioned in the budget of up to 20 or more that a person can have as a flexible alternative at age 60 to 71 to take the money out, but also the alternative where he puts the funds into a registered retirement investment fund. This would allow those people who are capable of looking after their own funds to even increase them during the period of pay-out.
The point I am concerned about is that it is not clear from reading the budget speech or the ways and means motion that the alternative of taking out a single payment has been retained for those who want it. It will be remembered by those who know the technique of the RRSP that at one time you could just take it out in a life annuity. Then it was amended in section 146 of the Income Tax Act so that you could take it out as a single payment. Those were the two alternatives.
In 1976, I asked the minister if he would consider more alternatives to give greater flexibility so that people would not be locked into limited choices but could get the money out in a way that suited them. The minister has kept the life annuity system which many people like-you can buy it from life insurance companies as you do now-and he had added two new ideas which are good. Now you are allowed to take a number of set payments. The third choice of the RRSP, namely the RRIF, is better for those who feel able to look after their finances from age 60 to 71 and into the future.
The Budget-Hon. Alvin Hamilton
I am concerned, however, that he may have taken out, inadvertently, the alternative of the single payment. Some people may want the freedom of taking out the money and paying the full tax. If we are to encourage people to save, I think we must do everything we can to make the plan as flexible as possible and give them a choice. I think this would bring more people into the plan. The primary aim is no longer just saving for the future but saving for the health of the nation.
I should like to commend these proposals to the government.
I am sure that after the next election they will be added to the plan. I cannot take away from the government, however, that they have done as I asked two years ago and I should like to thank them for that.
There are other proposals which I made in my speech in 1976 and one which was made by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). He suggested that when a person came to the age where he could take money out of the RRSP, if he wanted to he be allowed to add a church, some sort of university or any form of charitable institution to share the money instead of just a spouse. That would still give the individual the choice and the money would go some place where it would do some good under the tax law and help the country out as well. 1 think that should be added to the list of proposals I made two years ago.
There is another choice that the government should consider as well as the one advanced by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock. Banks, credit unions, trust companies and the like could hold the money, and then let the individual take it out at his convenience and pay tax on it. This would give maximum freedom to the individual. Some people feel uncertain about the future at age 60 to 71 and might like to postpone payment, or take smaller payments in the earlier years and larger ones as they get older when the costs of medical care are likely to arise. Individuals who have worked hard all their lives and done without recreation and holidays might like to spend a lot of money in the first years, on the other hand, and have less in later years. We should not be concerned about what the individual does with his money. He should have the choice as long as he pays income tax on what he receives. I think these additional proposals should be considered by the committee that works under the Minister of Finance when drafting future budgets.
I conclude these remarks by saying to the government once again that, as a member of parliament and as a Canadian, I appreciate the willingness of the Department of Finance to accept the positive ideas that bring improvements about.
Now I come to the bad news, Mr. Speaker. As I have said many times before in this House, I have watched ministers of finance take on the job with enthusiasm for the recognition and the great honour that the prime minister of the day has placed in them by giving them this onerous task. I have seen minister of finance after minister of finance go down the drain by being handed a budget to deliver in this House which in essence destroyed that minister. I saw it happen back in 1956. The Liberal minister of finance of that year disappeared

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Hon. Alvin Hamilton without a trace because of the unhappy budget of 1956. I have seen this happen to minister after minister. I have recited their names and what happened on previous occasions.
I asked this new minister, having great faith in his background, coming as he does from a small town where common sense is supposed to prevail, to try and avoid this type of fate for himself. Obviously he had the confidence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He had the confidence of this House because he was well liked and is well liked. But yet he had to bring in a budget the like of which we heard on April 10. Why this budget is bad is simple to explain. Essentially it is the same as the last four budgets, those of 1974, 1975, 1976 and 1977. The budgets of the last five years have been neutral budgets. They have tried not to go one way too far or the other way too far because of a particular mythology which is held like an article of faith by the financial advisers of the government. These advisers believe that there is a relationship which is contradictory-having unemployment on the one hand, and inflation on the other. The name for this mythology is the Philips curve. In using the Philips curve one tries to help the unemployed by doing things to make more jobs available but it increases inflation.
On the other hand, in trying to do things to reduce inflation it adds to the unemployed. This idea that one works against the other has been analysed and analysed over the last 20 or 30 years. Without any exception, to my knowledge, every analysis shows that by quantitative analysis this theory of the Philips curve is wrong.
Instead of simply ending my comments when I spoke to the minister on his mini-budget last fall, I put forward a sample idea of how the minister could fight both unemployment and inflation in the same move. I labelled that proposal "potential budgeting". I pointed out the precedent of 1964 that exists in the United States. At that time the situation there was very similar to the situation we have in Canada today. It was not as serious, but it was similar with much unemployment and rising inflation. They also had a budget deficit as we have now. The president at that time, President Kennedy, accepted the advice of his new adviser, Mr. Heller, and deliberately reduced taxes to the extent of $10 billion. This caused one tremendous uproar across the United States. But because those tax reductions were at a time when there was unemployment and unused plant capacity it precipitated a rush of work, thus giving people jobs. When the year was over the big gainer by $19 billion was the government of the United States. In other words, there was a situation which could only be described as taking advantage of the potential.
If one uses the theory of potential budgeting it must be recognized that it can only be used at a time when there is unused plant capacity and when there is available a labour supply. In providing tax reductions they must be aimed at those things which the country and the people need and which are not presently available. There is no use trying to encourage people to build more plant capacity when there is already more

plant capacity than needed. There is no lasting benefit in providing temporary jobs. That solves nothing. If tax incentives are put forward to produce things that people do not have and need, people will buy them.
I gave the minister one or two examples in that speech last November. He asked me then if I would present these ideas to him in written form. I did this in the form of a letter. In that letter I pointed out that these were not the end of all his problems but these ideas primarily were an example of where I thought we could provide $1 billion, a new year of production and consumption, and where the multiplier effect of two or three times would bring back to the various governments in Canada more money than the tax reduction had amounted to. When a tax reduction is given on items which people are not using and no longer making, there is no loss to the balance of ways and means. One simply says that if one does these things, there will be no tax or that the tax will be reduced so much. Therefore, it would not hurt the balance of ways and means, which the minister could not afford at this time with a big deficit.
However, it would provide these incentives to people to buy goods and have them produced and there would be a net gain. This net gain would show up not only in the wages of the people employed but also in the reduction of the social costs of unemployment insurance and social welfare. As these goods go through the system, the multiplier effect takes place and the various governments along the way would probably end up with $2 billion in extra revenue.
I think the minister was most impressed by my discussions with him but he had to take the matter up with his advisers. I will not quote his whole letter to the House, but I will quote two sentences because they say it all:
Your proposal would represent a major departure from the general policy of only permitting deductions with respect to assets used for the purpose of gaining or producing income. In my view, allowing deductions for such personal expenditures would create a dangerous precedent and might seriously erode the tax base.
I knew the minute I received that letter, which is dated March 2, 1978, that the minister had signed a letter written by his advisers who had turned down my proposal. In essence, my proposal was simply that on the 17 things I had listed which were needed and wanted by the people and the country and which were not being produced he should allow an individual in Canada to buy those items and then be allowed an exemption against income tax for the amount spent.
For example, if a person is asked to buy a heat pump to extract the heat out of the ground, out of water, out of the air, or even from a pile of rocks so as to heat his house, that person would have to spend in the neighbourhood of $1,000 to $3,000, depending on the type of equipment, size of his house, and so on. That means that by spending that amount of money, that person would eliminate the need to purchase oil and gas. He would be able to eliminate monthly and annual fuel expenses. His monthly charge would be replaced once and for all by a capital payment. If that man and his family were in business, every expense like this would be looked at under the Income Tax Act as the expenditure of money to make money, as the
April 19, 1978

minister points out. I suggested that the same privilege which is given to businesses to encourage them to spend money to make money be given to the individual homeowner or the man who owned a high-rise, or who owned a business establishment or any other form of business which could reduce the money spent on forms of energy which are becoming short in supply and more costly. You replace a monthly bill with a once and for all capital expense good for 20 or 30 years.
This proposal is not necessary for businesses because it is already in the tax law. However, there are four million, five million or six million homes in Canada that would immediately benefit if the minister had accepted that proposal. There are any number of high-rises where businessmen who own them could take advantage of it.
In any case, my point is simple. The minister signed a letter turning down this proposal, even though he himself personally liked it, on the ground that it would create a dangerous new precedent. Imagine treating an individual in Canada fairly, like you treat a business, being a dangerous precedent according to the financial advisers of the government! In effect, these very sincere individuals who know all the precedents have unwittingly destroyed that minister. Now he cannot go out and face the people of Canada, or even the people of his constituency, and say "I gave the individuals in this country the same treatment as we give to business. If a business goes out to save money by putting in new equipment, it can get a reduction; but if you as an individual do it, you cannot because I yielded to my financial advisers."
That is the key issue in all of our western democracies. Our governments have become so complex-governments are into everything today-that we have had to develop these huge advisory groups, in a simple word called a bureaucracy, who go on year after year and develop these great pyramids within the system. They are so used to funneling advice to ministers that they, in effect, become the decision makers.
The test today in our western governments of a minister, particularly the Minister of Finance who carries the can finally, is that the elected representatives of the people who go into the executive or the cabinet exert some control over this solidly entrenched bureaucracy.
On the basis of the principles I have put forward, I doubt whether 5 per cent of the people of Canada would object to that type of proposal. I know the minister did not object. He thought it was a good proposal. However, his advisers say it is a new precedent. When a business puts money into assets, that is a deduction. When an individual does it, that is a dangerous precedent.
I know the reason the advisers say that. They agree we will not lose any taxes on these 17 different items I listed, but they feel that somebody may come along and name another item that will save the individual money and people will ask for that same privilege to be applied to that item. I can accept the logic of that. However, I still say why not apply it?
The Budget-Hon. Alvin Hamilton
I can accept that in the national interest we have to save more money. People are doing that with RRSP's. It is not the only way, but it is one way that we do it. We not only have to save money out of our income, but we save money by looking after our affairs in such a way that our costs are less. To get at the root of this cost-push type of inflation we are suffering from, the government should not only encourage business to reduce costs, for which they give them incentives, but also it should give that inducement to individuals. This was the push of my proposal. This was the suggestion that I made, in a constructive way, I hope. The minister accepted it.
When the minister came in with the budget, and when he came in with that letter a month before the budget, I knew that the public servants were still in charge of the writing of the speech for the minister. Therefore, my heart, and I hope the heart of every politician, goes out to a very fine gentleman, the Minister of Finance, who really took it on the chin on April 10.
The minister knew that economically this country was in a bad way. He knew this country was not strong. He knew the people of this country were worried. Every time they picked up a newspaper, listened to the radio or television, they heard all the bad news.
The current thing is the shaky state of the dollar. The minister is not wrong when he says that he wants the dollar to float. That is a sound policy. However, once you let the dollar float, then inflation is purely a national matter, not an international matter. When you have a pegged dollar, inflation can be exported or imported, but not when you have a floating dollar.
The minute the minister came out with a policy of a floating dollar and allowed the public servants to sneak in and monkey around on the excuse they were stabilizing the ups and downs of the market, they helped destroy that minister. They created a state of uncertainty among those who invest or speculate in the currencies of various countries. They knew there was a possibility of making money on speculation.
If the dollar is floating freely, one speculator fights another speculator. The one who made the wrong guess would take a beating. That would stabilize it. However, when the Bank of Canada monkeys around and puts in blocks to slow the slide of the dollar, you create a situation of great uncertainty as to what the policy is which gives maximum opportunity for the speculators to raid the dollar.
The minister was forced to bring in a neutral budget. The only thing he did in trying to get at the question of costs was reduce the sales tax temporarily in order to get by the election. It will not have any more effect than the mini-budget of last fall or the budget of a year ago. When the facts come out and inflation, prices and unemployment continue to rise, the Minister of Finance will take the blame.
For five years we have had these neutral budgets because the public servant does not know what to do. He will not accept these new theories of potential budgeting. He will not accept any new precedents. The only thing he knows is what the precedents are.
4666

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Horner
This situation is not new. I happened to be minister of a government for five years or more and I saw the same things. We knew the advice we were getting from our financial advisers was wrong, but how does a group of ordinary MPs who have become cabinet ministers do anything about it? All you have is this one type of advice. Therefore, we proposed the setting up of an Economic Council of Canada where we could have people from the business world, labour and the academics sitting as a separate institution with their experts, looking at the economy from a completely unbiased point of view and yet representing the people who have to do the work to make this country run.
The Economic Council of Canada really did not get started until 1964. It has produced over a dozen reports. For years they have asked the government to consider potential budgeting. It is so bad that when the committee was meeting in the House three or four years ago, one of the public servants got up and in that committee meeting attacked the Economic Council of Canada for the colossal gall of advocating a new theory, even though that theory had been used in the United States in 1964 and 1965.
The head of the Economic Council of Canada disappeared. They moved in new ones more tame and amenable to the view of the Prime Minister. Today we witness the Economic Council of Canada, which was designed to give at least a second point of view to the government, being allowed to die. The bureaucracy is opposed to it. It attacks the heads of the Economic Council publicly, and it knows that the government is opposed to them too. Therefore, we see this fine institution, composed of volunteers, so to speak, from the business world, the labour world and the academic world, having its advice ignored by the government. The government goes the opposite way. The evidence of what I am saying about its dying is the fact that if we look at the number of people sitting on that council-there should be about 26 or 27-it is down to half that number now, and the government is just waiting for it to die and disappear entirely.
In conclusion, the tragedy of this budget debate is not that the country will not survive; we will change governments eventually. The tragedy is to see a human being for no good cause destroyed by having to accept advice which is wrong and which has been wrong for the last 30 years. That will be the issue upon which we will fight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before rising to participate in this budget debate I read some of the speeches. I have been unavoidably away for some of the debate, but I would like to deal with the budget and the economy of the country in the context of where we are in the manufacturing world, what some of our problems are and how we are attempting to solve them.
It has been said that one of the characteristics of Canadians is to downplay our achievements, to emphasize the negative and to exaggerate the problems. Certainly all three of those

things have been pretty evident in this debate. We have seen an abundance of this recently, not only in this debate but in many other places across Canada. I suppose in a way I will be attempting in this speech to redress the balance. It seems to me that it is of extreme importance that we as Canadians look at the whole picture, because without doing so nothing can really be achieved.
In common with the industrial world, Canada certainly has problems, but many of our problems have been exaggerated almost beyond recognition. As Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce I must be concerned, above everything else, about our international competitive position. Canada's prosperity clearly depends on our ability to sell our products in world markets. Whenever our costs and prices get seriously out of line with those of our trading partners, the nation as a whole is in trouble, and we were beginning to have problems on this score by the end of 1975 as far as our United States markets were concerned.
For several years before, the average increase in Canada's unit labour costs in manufacturing had actually been somewhat better than those of the United States. From 1967 to 1974, for instance, our labour costs in manufacturing increased by about 35 per cent. Those in the United States increased by about 43 per cent. This was offset, I suppose, to some extent by the rise in the value of the Canadian dollar during that period, so that by 1974 Canada's labour unit cost picture in United States dollars was slightly worse than the U.S. manufacturing picture.
The big disparities, however, really emerged in 1975. In that year unit labour costs in manufacturing rose by 16.4 per cent in Canada compared with 7.8 per cent in the United States, a sharp reversal of the picture between 1967 and 1974.
It was against this background that the program of prices and incomes controls was launched. Steadily, the growth of wage costs in manufacturing has been brought into line with that of the United States. In 1975, new wage settlements in manufacturing increased by 18 per cent in Canada compared with 10 per cent in the United States. These were in the first year of contracts. In 1977-and this is the point I want to make-new wage settlements for the first year of contracts were down to 7.6 per cent in Canada compared with 8.4 per cent in the United States. Surely, this is a remarkable achievement. 1 only hope that that trend continues, certainly now after April 14 when we began to remove wage and price controls.
Average hourly wage rates in manufacturing, however, continued to rise somewhat faster than in the United States in 1977, 10.8 per cent in Canada and 8.5 per cent in the United States. But what is even more important is that Canadian productivity in manufacturing increased by 4 per cent in 1977 compared with 2.2 per cent in the United States. That gives us some indication that our productivity is catching up in relation to productivity in the United States.
Even before adjusting for the exchange rate, our unit labour costs in manufacturing increased by somewhat less than they did in the United States, that is, by 5.7 per cent compared with
April 19, 1978

6.5 per cent. The depreciation of the Canadian dollar has had the useful effect of offsetting the extent to which our costs went out of line in relation to those in the United States in 1975 and 1976. By the end of 1978 we should be back in the position we were in in 1970 and 1971 with regard to manufacturing costs compared with those in the United States. The reason I am making this comparison with the United States is that Canada as a nation sells between 66 per cent and 70 per cent of what it sells in the American market.
It is clear that our manufacturing performance has recovered. Our productivity performance in 1977 was in line with our performance in the last 25 years. In that period of time manufacturing productivity in Canada increased by 158 per cent compared with 86 per cent in the United States. In other words, year by year the margin of productivity between Canadian and United States industries has been reduced, although some difficulties still remain.
There is another aspect of our competitive position which is widely ignored, and that is the steady improvement in our competitive position vis-a-vis industrial countries other than the United States. The point is that in general while our productivity has not increased as fast as it has in western Europe and Japan, our unit labour cost position has improved because inflation has been lower in Canada. Moreover, our competitive position in western Europe and Japan has improved further because of the rise in the value of their currencies vis-a-vis the Canadian dollar and the United States dollar.
The next major question about which I am concerned is the question of confidence in the business community, confidence in the consumer and confidence in the country as a whole. There is no doubt that in the last couple of years there has been a weakening of confidence throughout, I suppose, the whole industrial world. This can be seen by the advent of third world countries now acquiring tremendous wealth and becoming industrialized to some extent. People have become more uncertain about what the future holds for Canada, and there has been concern about the existence of Canada itself which has caused a great deal of apprehension and instability.
Perhaps it is natural that we should have periods in which the future looks bright and periods in which the future becomes cloudy and we become uncertain. I suppose it is inevitable that we have these periods in our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with interest to the statistics the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) has been quoting. They conform quite closely with the statistics I received two days ago from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) which were from the Department of Finance. They show that
The Budget-Mr. Horner
productivity rose very strongly in Canada during the period from 1968 to 1977. It rose almost 40 per cent during that decade, a growth which was 20 per cent better than that in the United States, which is somewhat in line with what the minister has been saying.
As I read those statistics, I remembered the statement the Prime Minister (Mr.Trudeau) made on October 19, 1977, as reported at page 32 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member will be able to make his speech in due time. If he has a question, would he please put it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to it, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister said:
We are only 80 per cent as efficient as the United States in our manufacturing sector ... We are 80 per cent as productive-
I wonder which statement the minister would like us to believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member has difficulty believing both of them, 1 could give him a lengthy explanation. Both are quite plausible. We have been considerably behind the United States in productivity for a number of years. We are gaining ground in productivity and making substantive gains because of the greater capitalization within our industry and our increasing ability to enter larger markets.
As I was saying, clearly we are entering a period when our confidence is increasing. There are a number of reasons for this. First, there is a renewed growth in the economy. In the last year, from the fourth quarter of 1976 to the fourth quarter of 1977 our economy grew at an average rate of 4 per cent. This is still less than is required to reduce unemployment, but it marks the beginning of a recovery. We expect a continued growth in 1978 amounting to about 5 per cent, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has stated on a number of occasions. Obviously business confidence has also been improved by the restoration of our competitive position and by the strength of our export performance, with commodity exports in 1977 22 per cent higher in volume than in 1975. I, as well as the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), have put these figures on the record on a number of occasions. We had a surplus in commodity exports of about $2.9 billion in 1977, which was a substantial increase over the 1976 and 1975 figures.
Business confidence is also improving because the business corporate profit position is moving back to more normal levels, with an increase of 19 per cent in 1977 in corporate profits after tax. Moreover, the corporate profits available for investment, that is after taxes and the payment of dividends, increased by 26 per cent in 1977. It is true that the business profit position is not yet back to what is required, but very significant gains were made last year.
I think that confidence is improving also because of the growth in employment. We hear a great deal about unemploy-
4668

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Homer
ment but, as the Minister of Finance has stated on a number of occasions, there has been a substantial growth in employment. It is true that unemployment continues to be much higher than I and many other members of the House would like to see, but we have brought about an increase in new jobs in the last year by 287,000, amounting to 1,391,000 in the last five years. In my view that is a substantial growth in a country with a population as small as Canada's.
One should look at the participation factor in our economy. It has never been higher than it is now. I would like to relate back to the war years, back to 1944 when Canadians had a common goal and a common enemy and everybody was making gigantic efforts to go out into the labour force and work. More women than ever joined the labour force and worked in factories and young people sought jobs. In 1944, the participation factor was 57.5 per cent. Today the Minister of Finance stated that it is 62.4 per cent. That gives us some indication of the number of people who are now participating in our economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my view this is a very significant factor which should be taken into account when one considers unemployment and the creation of jobs.
There are also indications of an improvement in consumer confidence. The Conference Board's surveys, for instance, have shown that consumers tend to increase their purchases over what they had intended earlier. With the additional stimulus provided by the budget, we would expect an increase in real terms of close to 5 per cent in consumer expenditures for 1978 as compared to only 2.8 per cent in 1977.
I mentioned earlier the improvement in corporate profits which lays the ground for a renewed growth in business investment. This should begin in 1978, but will certainly strengthen in 1979. However, it must be pointed out that the current level of business investment is, in fact, relatively high. Business non-residential investment in 1977 amounted to 13.7 per cent of the gross national product, about the same as in earlier years. The average from 1965 to 1975 was 13.8 per cent, and from 1970 to 1975 13.6 per cent.
Now let us take a look at the future of this country. Canada, as a major trading nation in the world, is dependent on the health of the economies of other countries and principally the United States economy. Therefore, the expectation that strong growth will continue in 1978 in the United States is reassuring. Moreover, it is to be hoped that there will be stronger growth in western Europe in 1978 than occurred in 1977. Inflation continues to be a major international problem, but Canada is faring far better than many other countries.
Now I would like to take a look at some of the charges that have been made, particularly by the media, that the province of Alberta did not benefit from the budget which was recently announced. It was said that since Alberta does not have a sales tax, they could not be compensated by the federal government for reducing it. Many newsmen asked me about this. I say that

I find the budget to be tremendously helpful to the province of Alberta.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Thank you. I hope it was evident to many Albertans as well as to people in British Columbia.
I have worked for four or five years to convince the Department of Finance that farmers owning family farms which are incorporated should have the privilege of passing their farms on to their sons, daughters and grandchildren without being burdened by the capital gains tax. This was finally understood and accepted and I was pleased to see it announced in the budget. I know that many farmers and ranchers in the province of Alberta are very pleased at this measure as well.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite right. I did that for every farm except those which are incorporated. Now I have succeeded in doing what I could not do on the other side.
I should like to say a few words now about the Hall report on railroads in western Canada. Mr. Justice Hall said in his report that 2,100 miles of railway track should be upgraded to what he termed the year 2000 standards. How do you get the railroads to get to work and invest in the upgrading of that trackage? The major track through the northern part of the constituency of Crowfoot has always been a concern of mine. I presented a brief to the Hall commission when it was studying the railway situation in the west urging them to retain that line, which they did. They recommended that it be upgraded. I was particularly pleased to hear the minister announce it in his budget address. It will be tremendously beneficial not only to the constituency of Crowfoot but to the whole of western Canada, because it will encourage railroads to reinvest and they will have an increased cost allowance in the upgrading of the railway system there. This should speed up the whole rationalization of the railway trackage in the prairies. Naturally I think also of the $100 million which the federal government in investing directly in railroads to improve the trackage and thus western Canada's ability to get its products to market.
The government has committed itself to $75 million direct investment, over the next five years, to improve railway trackage in western Canada.
Also there have been measures to encourage investment in the development of heavy oils in northeastern Alberta and
April 19, 1978

Saskatchewan. There are three distinct measures in the budget which would encourage a third tar sands plant in Fort McMurray. The increased depletion allowance from 25 per cent to 30 per cent will encourage the building of a heavy oil refinery in Cold Lake. That project is being proposed by Imperial Oil. It will be a $3 billion to $4 billion expenditure.
Pacific Petroleum is proposing another one in and around the neighbourhood of Hardisty, Alberta. That happens to be in the northern part of Crowfoot. I was pleased to have some input in encouraging the Minister of Finance to take into consideration speeding up the development of our heavy oils.
There is a third one on the drawing board by Husky Oil in the province of Saskatchewan. There is a royalty question regarding that one which has to be ironed out with that province. Husky Oil hopes to spend $600 million in the province of Saskatchewan for its heavy oil refinery. Pacific Petroleum expects to spend in the neighbourhood of $600 million, and Imperial Oil expects to spend $3 billion to $4 billion on its refinery. If we can get these projects moving along and if the decision can be made, they are tremendous projects which will encourage employment all across Canada in the building of these refineries.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The current level of the Canadian dollar will stimulate significantly our exports, as well as encourage Canadian industry to supply more of the domestic market. In other words, Canada should look at the opportunities for improvement in our trade position which is affected by the present exchange rate. I like to look ahead with considerable confidence. It would be foolish to ignore current problems. The country as a whole has faced up to the problems in the past few years. On the average, Canadians are richer today than they were in past years, despite heavy and high unemployment.
As Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I should outline some of the things we are attempting to do in my department. These things will benefit Canadian industry, our trade picture and small independent businessmen.
Much has been said about the textile industry in the province of Quebec, and whether or not the government has assisted that industry. Not only has this been said about the province of Quebec, but it has been said about other provinces as well. In the early part of April, an article appeared in the Financial Post. I should like to refer to that article to prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that the import controls on textiles assisted the textile industry. Investments in the first quarter of 1977 were up substantially in that industry. In part, the article reads:
Gemini Fashions of Canada, Ltd., a Winnipeg outerwear producer, is projecting a 35 per cent upswing in sales, spearheaded by a nearly 50 per cent increase in its exports to 17 countries.
That is a substantive improvement in the textile industry. The article continues:
Style Guild Ltd., a Montreal shirt manufacturer, reports a 25 per cent increase in fall bookings. Spring orders were so good it will be entering its fall
The Budget-Mr. Horner
season later than usual. Employment, though still below 1975 levels, has increased...
It continues:
Majdell Manufacturing Co., a children's sportswear producer in Montreal, has had its best spring ever and is projecting a 50 per cent increase in sales over 1977.
I could continue to quote from that article, but I put these examples on the record because of the representations some people have made that the federal government has not helped the textile industry right across Canada with its import controls and the encouragement of investment within that industry. My department has helped substantially in many other ways. We are prepared to help them further.
I have been involved in negotiations with the opposition in order to pass the bill quickly through all stages. There is a great mood for passing legislation now. I should like the Export Development Corporation bill to pass through the House quickly. That corporation is practically out of financing to ensure and guarantee loans to customers who buy Canadian manufactured goods. The Export Development Corporation began in 1969. One can look at its accelerated guaranteeing of loans, which has been tremendous. One can compare it to the export of manufactured goods and see that the Export Development Corporation has created markets for Canadian manufactured goods, and in that way created employment.
In my negotiations with Ontario members of the opposition,
I cannot understand why they are reluctant to assist me in the passing of that piece of legislation. In doing so, they know their action is very, very detrimental to the employment picture in the province of Ontario. What can one expect from the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)? On March 14, 1978, the hon. member and I were talking about de Havilland in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I indicated to him that de Havilland was a going concern which employed 3,700 workers. Also I indicated that de Havilland had on order 37 Twin Otters, 17 Buffalo aircraft, eight Dash-7 aircraft and so on.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe indicated that de Havilland was one of those Crown corporations which he would put out of business, if he ever got at the reins of government. He callously disregarded de Havilland, and would throw them out of the door with one sweep of his hand. When hon. members opposite rise in the House and concern themselves with unemployment, sometimes I think they are really not serious, especially when I hear them make remarks such as that in committee. These remarks by the hon. member for York-Simcoe affected labourers and workers relatively close to home. De Havilland operates in the city of Toronto, and the hon. member's riding is somewhat north of Toronto.
I should like to refer to what my department is doing with regard to the Enterprise Development Board. Individual boards have been set up in each province. These boards have the power to guarantee loans of up to $200,000 at chartered banks. If necessary, we are prepared to increase that to $300,000. The guaranteeing of loans over and above that amount must come before the national board. Under the

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Horner
Enterprise Development Board, approximately $101 million of guaranteed loans to Canadian industries have been approved. Direct grants of $19 million have been made to Canadian industries for increased productivity initiatives and new products to meet Canadian demand.
Much has been said about the Federal Business Development Bank. Continually we are attempting to encourage it to become more venturesome with risk capital. The number of authorizations for the last fiscal year was 9,800, which is more than a 5 per cent increase over the previous year. The amount of dollars authorized by the Federal Business Development Bank in the last fiscal year increased 10 per cent over the previous one. That is some indication of what is being done within my department to encourage Canadian investment and to encourage Canadian industry to meet Canadian demands.
Much has been said about the operation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. What about foreign investment coming into the country? If one looks at foreign direct investment in Canada one will see that in 1976 we had a deficit picture of minus $295 million. That was caused by a number of huge withdrawals, and I think particularly of Atlantic Richfield selling out and taking its money back across the line, as well as a number of other large companies doing the same. In 1977 we saw that situation reversed and we had an increase in direct foreign investment in Canada to plus $175 million. To me this is encouraging, and I am certain that in 1978 the trend which started in 1977 will continue.
The number of applications under the Foreign Investment Review Act has increased substantially. In each case we demand that before an application is approved the applicant prove to us that he will offer a significant advantage to Canada in the field of employment, a significant advantage to Canada in the field of investment and a significant advantage to Canadians in their right to participation in any takeover or new company coming into Canada.
We are doing a great deal within the department to encourage confidence in the Canadian industrial and manufacturing sectors. I want to deal briefly with the 22 sector studies we have set up within the department. For the first time we have brought business, labour and the federal and provincial governments together acting as a catalyst in a secretariat. They are studying the 22 major sectors within our economy to ascertain what stage they are at now, how large a market we can expect to gain in each of those sectors, and how we can obtain those gains. We are looking closely to see whether we can remove some of the duplication of tax structures that exist between federal and provincial governments, and we are looking closely to see whether-
