speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks for today by confirming that I am a member of the opposition in this House of Commons and I do not like the government we have across the way. In fact, I do not believe that Canada can stand that outfit much longer. My reason for saying that is that in a good deal of what I am going to say this afternoon I shall be remarking favourably about statements made by one of the members of the present cabinet. I am not referring to the minister who has just taken his seat. He would not want a kiss of death like that. I am referring, rather, to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
As she well knows, I referred in the Standing Committee on Health Welfare and Social Affairs, on Tuesday, April 4, to a speech she made on Monday, March 13, to the Sherbrooke Federal Liberal Association. The speech was entitled "The Myths of Social Policy". I told her in the committee that I have not been so excited when reading a document since the day many years ago when I first read Edward Bellamy's "Looking Backward". She is so young I do not think she knew what I was referring to, but the fact of the matter is, for a chart of what we ought to be doing in social policy in Canada today, that speech of the minister's on Monday, March 13, was indeed outstanding. I was able to persuade the committee that day to append it in its entirety to the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. It can be found as an appendix to issue No. 6 dated Tuesday, April 4, 1978.
I want to refer to a few things the minister said on that occasion, but before doing so may I say two other things. First, I think it should be required reading for every member of the Liberal party in this House of Commons and for every Liberal candidate who takes part in the forthcoming election, and, in particular, it should be required reading for every member of the present cabinet.
The other day the same minister made a speech during this budget debate which is to be found in Hansard for Friday, April 14, beginning at page 4528. Again, I wish to tell her that she made a very interesting and a very important speech, and I hope members of the Liberal party will read it. Indeed, I hope she is, by those speeches and the stand she is taking on social policy, causing at least a little bit of thought in the Liberal party so far as this whole field is concerned.
I shall paraphrase a few of her most important words rather than read them directly, because she did relate them to a specific item. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated the tone of both of those speeches, the one in Sherbrooke on March 13 and the one in the House of Commons on April 14, when she said words to the effect that
April 19, 1978

when one has a progressive concept it should not be lost in times of economic uncertainty. She went on to urge that people not panic and question the universality of some of our programs or their indexation to the cost of living or some other measure of monetary depreciation. I thoroughly agree with that sentiment and support it as strongly as I can. Just because the government says we are in difficult times or in times of restraint is no reason for saying that this practice of restraint has to be taken out in respect of our social programs or on the people in this country who benefit from those programs.
The theme I got from both those speeches by the minister, and it ran all through them, was that instead of talking curtailment of our social programs we should be expanding them. The speech that was made to the Sherbrooke Federal Liberal Association emphasized this point when the minister said that not only can we afford more equality, we must afford it.
I stand here today in full support of what this new Minister of National Health and Welfare is saying. I deplore as strongly as I can those who argue that there should be a falling away from the universality of some of our programs or that there should be cutbacks affecting old age pensions or family allowances or medicare programs. On the contrary, I agree with the sense of pride with which the minister referred to those programs that have been developed in the last few decades as some of the best programs that we have in Canada today.
The Prime Minister, whether it was in jest or something else, referred to my friend, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and myself as leftovers from the depression, but he certainly cannot say that about the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She is far too young to have any memory of the depression. She knows about it only from reading about it in the history books. However, she is aware, as a person who is alive today, of the fact that unless our society continues to exercise compassion and concern for all our people we are not worth the name "civilization" or anything else.
I shall now refer to that speech that the minister made at Sherbrooke, Quebec, on March 13. She started it quite openly by noting that in recent times there seems to have been a drift to the right. She noted the fall of certain social democratic parties in countries in Europe, and she also noted that the New Democratic Party had lost two governments in western provinces in the last two years. As I say, this was the theme of her speech: There is a move to the right and we had better face it. She goes on to say:
But there is a danger in all this too-a danger of which I have to be aware as Minister of National Health and Welfare, of which all of us should be aware as decent human beings.
What she is saying is that the danger of which we have to be aware is the drift to the right, particularly when that drift starts to attack social programs. She goes on:
That danger is that in the current swing of the political pendulum we will overlook the needs of millions of Canadians who are far less fortunate than we
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
are. It is after all, very easy to turn our backs on poverty, on the struggles of a deserted welfare mother with three or four children or of a young blind person or of the 55-year-old single man crippled by accident or disease, unable to work but not old enough to receive an Old Age Pension. It is all very convenient to turn our backs on the nearly 600,000 families in Canada who are poor in spite of the fact that they do work, many of them very hard indeed.
I emphasize the next sentence:
If we turn our backs on them we can hardly claim to be a society that believes in social justice or in the worth of dignity of humanity.
Later on, as she is going through that speech seeking to dispel all the various myths about social policy in these times, she dealt with a particular one in these words:
Another of the cherished myths to which Canadians hold-the fourth one on my list-is that the distribution of income in Canada is already too equal and that this is destroying the incentive to work.
I am not reading from some speech, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands or I made back in the 1930's. I am reading from a speech made this year by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare. Continuing:
To really believe that, one has to be quite blind to reality so please consider the actual figures. In 1977 the poorest 20 per cent of Canadian families received less than 6 per cent of total Canadian family income while the richest 20 per cent of Canadian families received 40 per cent of all the income. These figures are, unfortunately, very stable. The share of income going to our poor families has scarcely changed since the end of the second world war. It rises a bit in good economic times and falls in the bad, indicating that more affluent Canadians, whatever their good intentions, do make a habit of riding out recessions on the backs of the poor, but in general, the last 30 years have not seen significant redistribution of income.
This is not a speech left over from the depression, nor is it some street corner attack; this is a speech by the present minister speaking, out of her study and perception, on the problems facing many Canadians today. My hope is that this speech will be read by every member of the Liberal party in this House, and in particular by every member of the cabinet.
I have a few more lines that I would like to read from this Sherbrooke speech:
What this means is that Canada's poor families are getting along on an average of one-seventh of the income of families on the upper one-fifth of our population. You-
I gather that the "You" referred to the Liberals who were in the audience she was addressing in Sherbrooke.
You are likely all in that upper one-fifth. Divide your family income by seven and try to imagine what it would be like living on that one-seventh.
She goes on and refers to further statistics that are highly sophisticated and technical, but which show that Canada and the United States are twice as bad as the next worst country, Britain, and are far worse than Germany, Norway, Denmark or Sweden. She is referring to the way our income is distributed and how wealthy the wealthy are and how poor the poor are. Then she says:
Yet we happily go along punishing the poor while we cherish the comforting myth that we cannot afford any more equality.
I am still quoting the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare, and I emphasize the next word and the words that follow. She says:

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
Nonsense. Not only can we afford more equality, if we look at how well some of the more equal countries have done economically we could argue that not only can we afford it, we must afford it.
I have no qualifications to make in my praise of that speech made by the minister at Sherbrooke, Quebec, on March 13. It is a stirring call for all of us to realize that we have built up in this country over the last few decades measures of social policy that are good-and I am going to quote something she said in the House that underlines that point. But I realize that that minister is afraid that, because of the swing to the right and because of the calls for restraint, her own cabinet colleagues will yield to the pressure to cut back on those social programs. I am sure that she expresses the view, and I certainly express mine, that the answer to calls for restraint in times like these is to fight those calls with the call that really matters; namely, for more equality and for programs that will really get to and help all of the people of this country.
Not only was there that speech by the minister in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on March 13, but there is also the speech she made in this House on April 14 when she went over the programs we have developed and said:
Of course, numerous social programs which have been set up during the last decade or in the last fifteen years do not only benefit Canadians who are poor. Indeed, those social programs improve the quality of life of the vast majority of Canadians, which explains their being so popular.
Later she talks about another phase of the matter and says:
We are all richer for the fact that our society is compassionate enough to care for those of our people who need services like day care, rehabilitation, counselling or nursing home care. Even more directly, we are all made richer by the provision of universal access to complete medical care via programs instituted by federal governments over the last three decades.
I am so pleased with such statements that I do my level best to forget what the Liberals in this House were saying during the years we were fighting for improved social programs, fighting for hospitalization and fighting for medical care. I cannot really forget their opposition and the decades it took to persuade the Liberals to go through with the things they committed themselves to in 1919. Because we have this minister now saying that much of what is good for society is measured by the extent to which we have established income support programs, health programs, day care programs and programs that enable people to have a richer quality of life, I commend her and I am pleased to draw attention, as I am doing, to these two speeches of the minister, the one made in Sherbrooke on March 13 and the one made in the House of Commons on April 14.
I think it is clear that she means one should not lose a good concept in times of economic uncertainty and that people should not panic because there are attacks on programs of universality, and so on. I think we should be doing the very opposite and doing it in this House. That is why I am doing it today. The time has come to say, as some of us have been saying every chance we get, that what is needed today are improvements in the programs we have.

The Ontario Royal Commission on Pensions is meeting in this province. I know it is a provincial commission and thus not the responsibility of this government or this parliament, but I think we all ought to be interested in the briefs presented as it travels from city to city. The press has reported most of those briefs. I hope hon. members are aware that a number of themes run through the briefs, whether they come from the Canadian Labour Congress, pensions associations, individuals, or whatever. To a considerable extent the theme is that with all we have done to establish the universal old age pension, guaranteed income supplement, Canada Pension Plan and so on, there are still many thousands of older people having a difficult time getting by and that we ought to be increasing the basic amount of old age security.
The government must not give us the line that indexing by the consumer price index every three months keeps old people in a position that they can keep up with things. The amount of the pension is always behind and the amount it is based on was inadequate to begin with. The fact is that a substantial increase is needed and practically all the briefs presented to the Ontario royal commission, or all that I have noted, have said this.
They have also made a particular point of another matter which is a real concern of mine, the fact that older women seem to have a tougher time even than older men. Women in the 60 to 65 age bracket are finding things very tough, particularly with the spouse's allowance that does not do anything for those of single status. It is also true that women between age 65 and 75 seem to suffer the discrimination that women have suffered all their lives.
I do not accept the contention that because this is a time of restraint we should not be saying these things. In a time of restraint there should be more of an attempt to divide what we have. We should not be riding on the backs of the poor or of older people to try to get our economy going. I believe attention should be paid to these appeals that are being made, so I take my stand again in these so-called times of restraint for a substantial increase in the basic amount of old age security.
I contend that we should also do something right away about the position of persons between ages 60 and 65. The spouse's allowance helps a few, but very few. It is still based on the proposition that a woman can get a pension if she is in that bracket, provided she has a man. The fact that she may have a need or some other entitlement does not help her. It is wrong in every respect.
I think on some basis we should be getting the pension at age 60. The minister comes back at times and says persons between age 50 and 65 are in trouble. I am prepared to listen to some other ways of providing pensions for people in that bracket who need them, but let us not put it on a marital basis. Most of the people in that age bracket who are in need are women. It can be said that the spouse's allowance is an equal pension because it works either way, but most who get it are women. To the extent that we do not do something for the age bracket, whether 60 to 65 or 50 or 55 to 65, we are carrying
April 19, 1978

forward into later years the discrimination that women seem to have suffered all their lives.
I can mention plans like the railway pension, pensions of retired civil servants and those pensions that have not been escalated although others have-all those things should receive attention. We should also be doing something right away for our veterans. I was pleased to see that someone else has taken up the motions that my friend Jack Marshall used to move. We had one today from one of my friends to my right, calling for an increase in the basic rate of the war disability pension and the correction of the 48 per cent rule as it affects widows. I am sorry that someone on the government side said no to that motion. These things ought to be adjusted now. Let us not have the line that there is restraint. That was not the argument when these people joined up to serve the country, so let us not have that argument now.
Another thing I should like to refer to is the question of reciprocity in terms of agreements between this country and others. For a long time we expressed concern, particularly about United Kingdom pensioners in this country who do not get any escalation. We were told it was because there was no agreement and there was no legislative basis for such agreement. Last year we passed a bill which provides the legislative basis for an agreement between Canada and other countries with plans similar to ours. We are told that negotiations are still going on, but the people who are waiting for their pensions to be escalated are in many cases dying while they wait.
Medicare is one of the highlights of the social programs in this country. It is under considerable attack in this province at the moment because of the increase in fees that the government at Queen's Park is proposing. One hopes the discussions that are going on there and the minority situation in which the government finds itself may result in a resolution. It is not enough to keep and maintain medicare as it is. There are problems in terms of home care. Some of the provinces have moved way ahead in this field and there are provinces which are way behind. Surely we have reached the day where we can recognize the truth of the minister's statement which she made the other day. I shall read it again. It says:
We are all richer for the fact that our society is compassionate enough to care for those of our people who need services like day care, rehabilitation, counselling or nursing home care.
This is not a call for us to spend money or a call for us to be extravagant; this is a call for us to be a decent and compassionate society. That call is just as important in times of restraint as it is in times of affluence. That is why I was so appreciative of the speech which the minister made in Sherbrooke a month or so ago and again of the speech which she made in this House last Friday afternoon.
The other angle, of course, that is facing us is the question of a guaranteed annual income. I have been so nice to the minister up to this point that maybe I can still be her friend if I express a disappointment. It really annoys me to witness the number of times that she gets up and blames the provinces
The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
because we have not made any progress in terms of a guaranteed annual income. The leadership for these things should come from here. I regard this as just an excuse to say that the provinces are not willing. As a matter of fact, when there were three New Democratic Party provincial governments in this country at least there were three provinces which agreed.
Just before the 1974 election I remember being telephoned and asked by one of the officials in the Department of National Health and Welfare whether we would mind if the negotiations went on during the election so that progress could be made no matter which party came into power after the election. I certainly gave my approval to that idea. But all of the things this minister has been saying about our society being good for what it does for our people, about our society being good because it is a compassionate society, that it is a society which believes in justice, hinge upon what she said at Sherbrooke, that to increase the amount of equality and to increase the availability of a good, rich life to all our people we will have to crown our social legislation, our pensions, old age security, Canada Pension Plan, family allowance, medicare, housing programs and so on with a guaranteed annual income program. Because, as she says, the hundreds of thousands of people who are at work still do not have enough to enjoy life as the upper echelons in this country enjoy it. In my view, this is what a budget should have been all about, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in this important debate on the budget tabled last week by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). First I would like to congratulate him, because I think it is a remarkable budget, not only on the economic level, but also on many other aspects. I rise today in this debate to talk about a subject especially dear to my heart-federal-provincial relations. I would also like to correct the distortions and glaring misconceptions which the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) took the liberty of spreading yesterday with remarkable impudence concerning the federal-provincial perspective of the budget presented on April 10 by my colleague the Minister of Finance.
As many speakers before me have said, it is a budget which satisfies the short and medium term needs of the Canadian economy as they appear now, a responsible budget which aims

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
to spur consumption, and hence production, while slowing down inflation, an innovative budget which, notwithstanding the comments of the spokesman for the official opposition, represents a step towards closer federal-provincial consultation on budget matters.
In this regard, I would have more faith and confidence in the views expressed by Ontario finance minister Darcy McKeough than in those of the Conservative opposition in the House, which in the last week has endeavoured to find faults in all the federal-provincial aspects of this budget. And contrary to the Conservative members in this House, here is what the finance minister of the Ontario Conservative government had to say before the provincial legislature on April 10. Dealing with the budget introduced by the Hon. Jean Chretien, Mr. McKeough said, and I quote:

It contains a major new federal-provincial initiative to stimulate the Canadian economy and improve confidence across the country. This short-term and shared-cost action represents a significant first in fiscal policy co-ordination in Canada. Ontario has played an important role in the design, development and implementation of this proposal.
That is the view expressed by the Conservative minister of finance for Ontario. I would hope that the Conservative opposition in this House would take the trouble to listen. If they do not want to listen to us. I would ask that they listen to a man of experience and knowledge, and to good politicians too who are at the provincial level in their party but not in this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give some consideration to the outbacks. [Translation]

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A budget which is not only innovative, Mr. Speaker, but at last a budget whose overall thrust is consistent with the positions unanimously endorsed and proclaimed by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and his provincial colleagues at the end of last February's economic conference. I should say unanimously minus one, since the premier of Quebec had chosen by then to act as a sulky child, to back out at the last minute and not to endorse the final communique of the conference.
The reason for that unreasonable gesture is quite transparent. Chances were the conference would have shown the people of Quebec and of the other provinces that Canadian federalism can function harmoniously and lead to co-ordinated federal and provincial policies, provided all governments show good will and good faith. Now, there is nothing insulting to the Quebec government in saying it is a separatist government. It is therefore in its interest to block systematically every federal-provincial agreement or consensus in the hope that it can thus convince Quebecers that federalism does not work and never will.
Therefore, Mr. Levesque, at that first ministers' conference, left the conference room, slamming the door. Again it was to promote the cause of separatism, as I shall show shortly, that the present finance minister refused for three weeks to say

whether or not he was in favour of reducing the sales tax accross-the-board as a step to give new impetus to our economy. For three weeks, Mr. Speaker, he was unable to give an answer, unable to decide whether such a step should be taken or not. His silence had but one purpose, at least the only logical one I can imagine, and that was to allow Mr. Levesque to commit another of his flights of language, through which he tries to stay in the public eye if not to keep his popularity with the electors, and to scream rape and prostitution and put forward a counter-proposal which tries to create the illusion that Canadian federalism cannot work. Once again his mano-euver is obvious, transparent. Obstacles are put in the way to keep the Quebec cart from going forward, and then right and left there are cries saying it got bogged down in the federal ruts. And, as usual, hon. members opposite swallowed it all, hook, line and sinker.
That is why, as the right hon. Prime Minister pointed out recently, the position stand they chose to adopt on the matter is wrong. We do not doubt their sincerity, but we have good reason to doubt their political acumen. In that regard, the unbelievable speech committed yesterday by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) quite astonished me.
As usual when she deals with federal-provincial relations, the hon. member peered at the sales tax issue through her bifocals. The big bad federal government was cast by her in the darkest, most sinister perception. The poor little provinces were seen through the rosiest of rose-coloured glasses.
One heard the hon. member refer to Alice in Wonderland although she added two new characters to Lewis Carroll's famous fairy tale, the big black federal bobcat and the big provincial flamingos. The hon. member seems to think the provinces can do what they want, when they want and how they want without any obligation whatsoever to consult with the federal government even in areas such as budgetary planning, which has obvious implications for both our orders of government. Thus ten provincial budgets were recently tabled without provincial treasurers bothering to consult with the Department of Finance, even in general terms, on the budgetary options open to them and their respective economic implications for the Canadian economy as a whole. I have not heard the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) complain about that.
On the other hand, it often appears that the sensitivity and consideration which the hon. member would want the federal government to apply to federal-provincial relations would prevent that government from doing anything, even in areas under its exclusive jurisdiction, unless all provinces had previously signed a formal agreement on the dotted line.
Such is the tale we were served yesterday by the official opposition. It can only be dismissed by anyone the least bit familiar with the political realities of federal-provincial rela-
April 19, 1978

tions as electoral posturing. In fact, I am tempted to paraphrase Lewis Carroll and call it "Flora in Postureland". Why posturing? Because the hon. member purports to agree with the government's approach to federal-provincial relations and then distorts and misrepresents the facts on the sales tax issue in her fruitless attempts to show that we do not practice what we preach.
The hon. member says that federal-provincial co-operation must be a two-way street. We agree. We have said that many times and we have practised it. She says there should be an input from the provinces in federal decision-making. We agree, although we would like her to add in order to be consistent with the statement to which I have just referred that there should also be a federal input in at least some provincial decision-making.
The hon. member says that in areas of shared interest or joint jurisdiction the federal government should not adopt a take-it-or-leave-it attitude. Again, we agree. She says that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should have taken his cues for the budget from the February first ministers' conference. The government fully agreed with that and the Minister of Finance did so.
What is all the fuss about? The fuss is about the Tories clutching at every straw in the wind to avoid being blown away in the next federal election.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not have to clutch at straws to show that, in the matter of sales tax, not only were the provinces consulted, but their views had a decisive influence on the substance of the budget tabled on April 10 by the Minister of Finance.
The notion that the reduction in sales tax could well be the most effective stimulus in the country at this juncture did not come out of the blue. It has been the object of public discussion in Canada for over a year. It was broached by my colleague the Minister of Finance at a meeting with his provincial counterparts last October. It was raised again by some provincial representatives at the December federal-provincial conference of finance ministers preparatory to the first ministers' economic conference. The arguments in favour of this measure have been vigorously and publicly rehearsed through these months by prominent members of the business community and the treasurer of Ontario, among others.
No attempt was made at the first ministers' conference to deal with, or come to agreement on, the specifics of budgetary planning. Government leaders rather sought agreement on broad principles which would guide and harmonize their action in the medium and long term. One such agreement was on the need to ensure that-and I quote from the final communique of the conference:
-the trend of government expenditure growth should be held, on average, to less than the trend growth in the value of the g.n.p. or gross provincial product.
As a result, the Minister of Finance announced in his budget speech that the expenditure ceiling previously set by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) for fiscal year
The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
1978-79 had been lowered by $350 million. Most provincial budgets similarly reflected this federal-provincial agreement on expenditure restraint.
The tax concessions proposed by the Minister of Finance for research and development expenditures, oil recovery systems, upgrading plants and earned depletion for non-conventional projects also reflected concerns expressed by the provinces at the first ministers' conference. As for the tax advantage extended to railways, it responded to concerns privately expressed by provincial representatives, both at the first ministers' conference and at meetings preparatory to it.
But the first ministers also agreed at their February meeting that-and I quote again from the conference's final communique:
-the general instruments of monetary and fiscal policy should be used to encourage the growth of demand which would bring the desired growth of output and employment, at declining rates of inflation.
It was from this agreement that my colleague the Minister of Finance took his cue in proposing to the provinces a jointly-financed reduction in sales tax. It soon appeared that this fiscal instrument was by and large the most appropriate one to achieve both accelerated growth in demand and lower inflation rates.
Having tentatively reached this conclusion, the Minister of Finance and his officials initiated what are probably the most extensive pre-budget federal-provincial consultations ever in our financial history.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They did that not only by telephone, although I cannot understand the excitement, worry and concern of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands about using the telephone as a system of communication. In any event, it was not only through telephone calls, as the hon. member suggested yesterday, but also through a series of meetings with provincial counterparts.
So that everyone will know, particularly opposition members, I would like to put on the record the chronology of these consultations. On Thursday, March 23, the Minister of Finance discussed the sales tax proposals by telephone with Mr. McKeough of Ontario and Mr. Parizeau of Quebec.
On Friday, March 24, the minister was in contact with Mr. Parizeau to discuss the sales tax proposal and other issues.
On Monday, March 27, the Monday right after Easter, the deputy minister of finance got in touch with all his provincial counterparts, with the exception of Mr. Collins of Alberta, where there is no sales tax, as hon. members know. The proposal was elaborated upon and discussed by finance officials on Monday afternoon, and a series of meetings was arranged for Wednesday.
On Tuesday, March 28, arrangements were completed for meetings with provincial officials on Wednesday. By this time the Minister of Finance had tried to contact all provincial

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
ministers of finance and had spoken with all of them, with the exception of those for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
On Wednesday, March 29, the minister travelled to western Canada for discussions with his counterparts in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia and with their officials. The minister telephoned Mr. Leitch, the minister of finance of Alberta. Finance officials met with the four deputy ministers of finance of the Atlantic provinces in Halifax and with the Quebec deputy minister of finance in Quebec City. Ontario officials met with the federal deputy minister of finance in Ottawa, and the latter also spoke with the deputy minister of finance of Alberta.
Then on Thursday, March 30, the federal Minister of Finance met with Mr. McKeough and Mr. Parizeau in Montreal. Mr. Parizeau was to call back on Friday, March 31.
On March 31 the minister tried to contact Mr. Parizeau, but was told that he could not be reached.
On Saturday, April 1 and Sunday, April 2, officials confirmed a meeting of officials on Monday in Ottawa, and work proceeded in the department on the preparation of material for the meeting. The minister of finance of British Columbia, in discussion with the federal Minister of Finance, stated that instead of adding one point for six months to the two points to be Financed by the federal government, British Columbia would prefer to add two points for a further three months.
On Monday, April 3, a meeting was held in Ottawa with representatives of all provinces to discuss the proposal further. A consensus emerged from the meeting that alcoholic beverages for home consumption should not be included. It was also recognized that in all provinces, with the exception of Newfoundland, tobacco products are taxed under separate legislation and should therefore be excluded. In Ontario amusements are taxed under the retail sales tax act, and Ontario officials indicated that they would prefer to exclude amusement taxes from the arrangements.
From Tuesday, April 4, to Friday, April 7, the Minister of Finance discussed the matter with Mr. Lyon, premier of Manitoba, who was in Ottawa. New Brunswick delivered its budget on Tuesday. During this period the minister was constantly in contact with provincial ministers and spoke with some of them on several occasions. He advised them that it would be desirable if they would be ready to respond to his offer should he decide to present a budget. This enabled both Manitoba and British Columbia to take the proposal into account in their budgets and to present them on the same date as the federal budget.
The deadline for completing budget preparations was Thursday evening. By this time all provinces, with the exception of Quebec, had agreed to the proposal.
On Monday, April 10-budget day-the minister telephoned all provincial ministers before delivery of the budget to confirm his proposal and officially seek their responses. Only Mr. Parizeau indicated that he would disclose his answer within a few days. All the others gave a positive response.

Is this lack of consultation? Is this a take-it-or-leave-it attitude? How can the opposition seriously talk about lack of federal-provincial consultation? How can hon. members opposite talk about paternalism and take-it-or-leave-it attitudes? Never in the history of this country has there been a federal budget in which there has been more honest, clear and precise consultation with the provinces.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands likes to refer to press articles. I suggest to her that she refer to an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of April 14 which I think summarizes the situation extremely well. It says:
Mr. Levesque and his finance minister aside, the country should be applauding the co-operation between Finance Minister Jean Chretien and his provincial colleagues. As the proportion of tax dollars controlled by Ottawa continues to shrink (it is now down to 40 per cent), so does the ability of the federal government to influence the course of the economy. Intelligent, non-partisan collaboration is required in these times.
Mr. Chretien believes that the good spirit developed at the so-called economic summit was the reason he was able to achieve such general agreement on the sales tax idea. That encounter certainly helped. The country is fortunate that provincial leadership, Quebec excepted, is now probably in the hands of more reasonable, moderate men than at any time in Canadian history.
Mr. Chretien sought and received help, and all Canadians should applaud that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry that only the opposition in this House seems to be unable to applaud such a development.

Mr. Speaker, there was never any rigidity nor any paternalism in our relations with the provinces on that subject. The consultation that has taken place was more than just a series of quick phone calls. The meetings I have indicated in the file and which cover an 18-day period should satisfy any honest person that extremely comprehensive consultation has taken place during the whole period between the Minister of Finance and his counterparts of the various provinces.
This is certainly not a question of taking it or leaving it since, like all other provinces, Quebec had 18 days to suggest changes. In fact, Saskatchewan and British Columbia did so and the Minister of Finance accepted them and took them into consideration in his budget. Only the Quebec finance minister was unable to come to a decision even insofar as accepting or refusing a proposal as simple and as elementary as this one. I should note that had Quebec said no at any time during these discussions, the Minister of Finance would certainly have re-examined his proposal and reconsidered the whole issue.
But how can there be normal federal-provincial relations when a government like that of Quebec simply seems to play hide-and-seek and tries to prevent the system from working? If at times we reach a stalemate in this area, the blame does not rest with the federal government but with the Quebec government which is doing everything it can to prevent federalism from working.
April 19, 1978

Mr. Speaker, the federal government has never suggested and is not suggesting now that the retail sales tax is its responsibility. Provincial authorities set and administer this sales tax, they are the ones who must decide what type of sales tax they want to collect, whether they want to increase them, reduce them, or increase them across the board or selectively.
In this budget, we have offered to share the cost of reducing the sales tax in the various provinces without any product discrimination, and all the provinces except Quebec have accepted this offer. Like I said earlier, even after three weeks of consultation the Quebec government was unable to make up its mind before the presentation of the federal budget on April 10. Since then it has come to the conclusion which we all know and which prevents Quebec from being eligible for the total sum that we have provided in our budget in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, the offer of the Government of Canada remains on the table and we do not intend to withdraw it. Since the Quebec finance minister took his decision, the federal government has already indicated its willingness to consider some changes to this formula if necessary. For example, we would be prepared to consider that the provincial contribution of 1 per cent not be required on each and every item or product which could benefit from the federal contribution of 2 per cent, and that the provincial government might reallocate as it pleases its contribution to restrict it to some products only.
Mr. Speaker, I shall add that the government is still prepared to consider, after consulting the other provinces concerned since Quebec is not the only province involved in this matter, any other sales tax arrangement the government of Quebec could propose provided it does not have the effect of using federal funds to break up the Canadian common market.
Mr. Speaker, I shall add that as federal government we shall make every possible effort to prevent the people of Quebec from being penalized in comparison with the people of Canada as a whole, because of the lack of co-operation on the part of the Quebec government with the federal government and with the other provinces. The people of Quebec are affected enough by the negative effects of the separatist options of the government which has been in power for two years in that province.
Mr. Speaker, my time is almost up. I would simply like to stress once again that in this matter the federal government took all the action that could be expected to come to an agreement with all provinces. For the reasons I indicated the Quebec government did not want to co-operate in the time frame available. Nonetheless, I repeat, we are still willing to continue to co-operate and to try to invent solutions which will be fair for the population of Quebec and for Canadians as a whole. But that requires that the other side have something else in mind than preventing the federal system from working.
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity to speak on the budget which was presented on April 10. It is a budget which will not bring any great change in Canada's economy or in the rate of unemployment. How can anyone take seriously the budget presented by this government which is spending $1 billion more a month than it takes in? The facts speak for themselves. It is ridiculous, and it shows what an irresponsible group of individuals they are who would allow such a situation to come about. They are telling us that this budget will create a miracle with temporary sales tax reductions. We will see absolutely no improvement in the record of unemployment or in the economy of this country.
I will be checking very closely the remarks made by the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) who gave his version of the consultations with the premiers, and I will be checking it out with the premier of Manitoba.
I have to laugh at the comment made by the minister that we do not practise what we preach. The most classic example of the government not practising what they preach is contained in a document that has been printed recently entitled "A Legacy of Spending". The author is Edward Murphy of CJOR, a radio station in Vancouver. He has the government's ten year dismal record here. It shows how the Canadian taxpayer has been taken to the cleaners like no other taxpayer. Mr. Murphy states on the first page:
On Wednesday, August 13, 1969, Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau went on national television in a major press conference to talk to the Canadian people about inflation and the country's financial future. He said this: "We would be on the way to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control. To spend vast sums on welfare, education and other programs while allowing inflation to continue would merely place hundreds of thousands of Canadians on a treadmill they could not escape."
The Prime Minister also committed his government to a substantial cut in the federal civil service. What has happened since August 13, 1969 ...
Government spending increased by .. .
It increased by 410 per cent, or over $35 billion.
Federal civil service increased by ... 45 per cent.
How could anyone take this government seriously? Their word means absolutely nothing. The whole history is in here. I cannot read it all, but one thing that really annoys Canadians no end is the ridiculous Canada Council grants. I would like to read one classic one: $170,000 to study air breathing fish of the Amazon river. How ridiculous can you get? How can anyone take this government seriously? Another grant of $17,700 was given to carry out a dialectological survey of the French language spoken in eastern Canada. Here is another one: $7,605 to study the economic basis of Machiavelli's political thought. Good heavens! How could we take this budget seriously? What kind of an elected official would hand out taxpayers' money like that?
There are other examples of grants to different publishing companies. I would not dare read out in this House the words

April 19, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
which are written out in these poems that have been compiled and paid for with taxpayers' money. Here is one in language which can be read out in the House:
Mix Mix Tom Mix
Mix Mix Tom Mix
Mix Mix Tom Mix
This goes on for about 25 paragraphs. Canadian taxpayers paid money to someone who does not want to work to compile this ridiculous nonsense.
There are many concerned Canadians who are putting out publications. Here is one on the cover of which is written: "Pierre Elliott Trudeau . . . You have failed ... miserably! The Trudeau Record, 1968-1978". In the opening pages the author, Michel Robert, states:
Who am I to write this book? A nobody! Just an ordinary but concerned citizen. But it is high time the nobodies of Canada speak out loud and clear.
The government will be hearing more from the nobodies because they are fed up. In fact, they are so fed up that they are willing to spend their own money to publish documents such as the one by Michel Robert.
The book continues:
As a matter of fact, there are many Canadians that think that Pierre Trudeau is deliberately creating economic chaos in Canada to prove that the system does not work and to gain sympathy for his socialist cause.
That is a very devastating and strong statement. We must look at the record unemployment, debt borrowing and uncontrolled spending. Those records do not indicate good management of the country. The facts speak for themselves.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) commented upon the government and politicians turning their backs on the blind, crippled and underprivileged. I want to assure the hon. member that no one in the Conservative party will turn his back on the blind, the handicapped or the poor. We made this perfectly clear during the 1974 election campaign. We pointed out in our prices and incomes program that over five million Canadians were below the poverty line, and that it was important to bring inflation under control in order to help these people. They are still below the poverty line and still suffering under the same government which has been in power for the last 15 years.
I was amused by the Liberal speeches yesterday which praised the government for the budget and indicated how wonderful the last ten years have been. I do not know how such statements could be made. Our standard of living dropped from second position down to tenth. How can the government indicate that it has done a good job? The evidence indicates a good job has not been done. It is unbelievable what has been accomplished by the government.
Many Canadians are leaving this country, and much investment money is leaving as well. I should like to deal with that in some detail. Canada is no longer an attractive country to invest money in. If the government was good and managed its affairs properly, investment money would be attracted and

investors and their money would remain here. That is not the case. This government is helping out an economy; it is assisting the American economy. The government is the best friend the United States has ever had. There is a real boom in Florida and California, and Kentucky is now calling itself the eleventh province because so many Canadians and Canadian firms are moving to that state. I did not hear any of the Liberals mentioning those facts yesterday. Neither did I hear any of them say how they propose to stop this outflow of capital and attempt to keep Canadian businesses here. The government's make-work projects such as Flip will not make up for this.

speechtext: Stop interrupting.

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Another thing which is driving business out of Canada is the 3,300 orders in council which were implemented last year. The government has caused much uncertainty in the country. These problems did not exist before. Liberal members talked about the last ten years and praised the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who has the most disgraceful record of any politician in Canada. In April 1968 there were 375,000 unemployed. Today there are well over a million. The unemployment rate in 1968 was 4.5 per cent. Today it is around 8.3 per cent.
Youth unemployment is another real problem in Canada. In 1968 the rate was 7.4 per cent, and today it has doubled to 14.8 per cent.
The record in Quebec is very dismal. In 1968 unemployment in the province of Quebec was 5.9 per cent. Today it is 10.9 per cent. Under the aegis of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), total unemployment has practically tripled. Approximately ten years ago Canada had an unemployment problem in only a few areas, but today it has spread right across the country.
I should like to refer to some statistics regarding the differences between Canada and the United States. Over the past ten years, our deficit has increased 11.5 per cent. In the United States, where some control and some sound management is being exercised, it is only 2.7 per cent. In Canada expenditures have increased 3.9 per cent, and in the United States 2.4 per
April 19, 1978

cent. The deficit expenditure rate in Canada rose from 7.3 per cent to 22 per cent, which is indicative of complete and total mismanagement of the nation's economy and the taxpayers' dollars. The deficit expenditure rate in the United States fell from 16.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent. The Americans are attempting to control government spending. This is necessary if inflation is to be cured.
Returning to the matter of investment leaving Canada, in 1976 this question was raised, first by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). At that time he pointed out that it was becoming a very serious problem. Also he indicated a very serious political climate was being created, and this trend of investment and business leaving the country was commencing. I received some documents from an investment
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
councillor in Winnipeg, Mr. Peter Henry Jerch. Mr. Jerch is working on behalf of 64 Canadian companies that are planning to move out of Canada and expand their facilities in the United States. This is a clear indication that the business community has no faith in the government or the country. There is no way any of the government's short-term projects will counter the mass movement of business investment money which is occurring.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
